title: Differential and Common Decoherence Modes in Witnessing the Quantum Gravity-Induced Entanglement of Matter
authors: Ryan Rizaldy, Helen M Sheehy, Tian Zhou, Anupam Mazumdar
abstract: In the context of the QGEM (Quantum Gravity-induced Entanglement of Masses) experiment, we consider two adjacent matter-wave interferometers in linear and parallel configurations that interact solely via gravity. If gravity were quantum, then the two matter-wave interferometers would become entangled via the virtual excitation of the massless graviton. In this paper, we consider witnessing this entanglement by considering a generic experimental scenario where the two interferometers are subject to different global phases and different decoherence rates. In this context, we show that the individual global phases do not affect the witness, discuss common and differential decoherence modes, and perform the parameter search optimal for different masses. We provide a mathematical framework for these asymmetric decoherence rates and then search for parameters that determine the entanglement witness. We have kept the inter-separation distance between the two closest superpositions of the interferometers' masses fixed while varying the experimental time from $τ=0.1$ s to $τ=1$ s. Finishing the experiment at $ τ=0.1$ s has many advantages from the point of view of protecting the experiment from random acceleration noise. However, witnessing the entanglement also suffers from $\langle W\rangle \sim -{\cal O}(10^{-2})$ for $m=10^{-14}$~kg, for decoherence rate in the ranges of ${\cal O}(10^{-1}-1)$~Hz for $τ=0.1$ s experiment. However, as we show, increasing the mass of the matter-wave interferometer may improve the witness considerably.
summary: This theoretical paper develops a framework to detect entanglement generated between two matter-wave interferometers via hypothesized quantum gravity interactions. It uses the entanglement witness derived from the partial transpose criterion, showing that the detectability of this entanglement is highly dependent on the mass of the test particles and the management of environmental decoherence. The results suggest that increasing the mass is crucial for achieving a measurable signal.
main_problem: The paper addresses the theoretical challenge of detecting entanglement generated between two matter-wave interferometers due to hypothesized quantum gravitational interactions.
main_result: The entanglement witness, derived from the Positive Partial Transpose (PPT) criterion, is shown to be sensitive to the mass of the interferometers and the decoherence rates, suggesting that increasing mass significantly improves detectability.
method: The analysis employs quantum information theory tools, specifically calculating the eigenvalues of the partial transpose of the density matrix ($ho^{T2}$) to quantify entanglement.
model_or_system: The system consists of two adjacent matter-wave interferometers (e.g., using nanodiamonds) whose interaction is mediated solely by gravity. The evolution is treated as an open quantum system subject to global and differential decoherence rates.
key_observables: The entanglement witness $\langle W angle$ (negative value indicates entanglement) and the entanglement phase $\phi_{ent}$.
important_parameters: Interaction time $	au$ (e.g., 0.1 s to 1 s), matter-wave mass $m$ (e.g., $10^{-14}$ kg to $10^{-13}$ kg), and common/differential decoherence rates ($\Gamma_c, \Gamma_d$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the density matrix can be factored into unitary (phase) and decoherence parts, and it models decoherence using effective common and differential rates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical setups (parallel and linear configurations) and show parameter scans of the entanglement witness $\langle W angle$ as a function of decoherence rates ($\gamma_1, \gamma_2$).
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the physical setup and the entanglement witness criterion, to deriving the density matrix evolution under decoherence, and finally calculating the eigenvalues of the partial transpose to determine the conditions for entanglement detection.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics as it applies advanced open quantum system techniques (decoherence modeling, entanglement witnesses) to a cutting-edge, fundamental experiment involving matter-wave interferometry and quantum gravity effects.
